newsitem.title: CHINA: HK to show colours in labour rights showdown.
newsitem.headline: HK to show colours in labour rights showdown.

text.p: Hong Kong's China-appointed parliament is set to show its colours in a showdown with unions over a bill that would scuttle labour rights laws.

The Provisional Legislative Council, due to meet late on Wednesday, was widely expected to strike down five of seven laws enacted shortly before China took back the 156-year-old British colony on July 1.
The issue is one of several entangling the post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa and his government and unelected legislature in constitutional polemics.
The other quarrels are over his plan to harden up sedition laws, his bill to deport child illegal immigrants and an election law blueprint that would hamper pro-democracy forces.
Wednesday's debate and vote seemed certain to test the mettle of Hong Kong's embryonic free trade union movement led by pro-democracy firebrand and ex-legislator Lee Cheuk-yan.
It would also set a precedent.

If the new legislature can roll back one set of pre-handover laws passed by the disbanded, elected Legislative Council, it could possibly attack a whole raft of old legislation, political analysts said.
The government wants the labour laws suspended for several months to give it time to table counter-legislation, arguing that the laws will harm Hong Kong's economic competitiveness.

The key rights that will go out of the window are the right of unions to bargain collectively with employers on wages and benefits on behalf of employees, and the right to use union funds for political activity. Unions and pro-democracy groups called a protest march for Wednesday afternoon and planned to hand a petition to Tung's office opposing the planned suspension of labour rights.

Lee, a former elected legislator who was ousted along with the rest of the pro-democracy bloc when China installed the provisional legislature on July 1, said he did not expect to win the present showdown but he vowed to keep up the fight.

"Within the establishment now -- both in the provisional legislature and the Executive Council -- are predominantly business interests," said Lee, secretary general of the Confederation of Trade Unions.

"So we are not too optimistic that it is possible to stop the suspension of the laws. But it's very important to keep the debate going and that the workers' voice can be heard in the community, so there can be a balance," he said on local radio.
"It's not just labour laws that are concerned. It's the defence of the elected Legislative Council's decions.

"One should not be choosy about defending only one law, one should defend all the laws. It's a matter of democracy and the rule of law. Laws should not be twisted around by the administration when they don't like them."
A leading Hong Kong economist has dismissed the government's arguments about a threat to competitiveness.
"They are not beasts threatening economic prosperity...but practices accepted worldwide," Tsang Shu-ki, a professor at Hong Kong Baptist University, told the South China Morning Post newspaper.

The rights enshrined in the jeopardised laws are in line with international labour conventions. Hong Kong's constitution, the Basic Law, says the territory should apply standards set in those conventions, and some legal experts say the suspension could spark a constitutional crisis.
